subject: physics
title: Discovery of the electron
key_idea: Cathode rays are streams of electrons. A hot metal releases electrons by thermionic emission, and a pd accelerates them. Thomson's measurement of e ÷ mₑ showed the electron is far lighter than any atom, and Millikan's oil drops showed that charge comes in units of e.

blocks.text: This section covers where the electrons come from and how fast they travel.

items: A discharge tube holds a gas at **low pressure**, with a very high voltage between two electrodes.
Rays leave the negative electrode, the cathode, and travel to the positive electrode, the anode.
The rays make the glass or a screen glow, and they cast a sharp shadow of an object placed in the way. So they travel in straight lines.
Electric and magnetic fields deflect them in the way a stream of negative charge would be deflected.

items.meaning: The release of electrons from the surface of a heated metal.

items: A current through a filament heats the cathode.
Some free electrons in the metal gain enough energy to escape from the surface.
In a vacuum an anode at a positive potential accelerates the emitted electrons across the gap. This is how an electron gun works.

diagram.question: An electron is accelerated from rest through a pd of {V} V. Calculate its speed in units of 10⁶ m/s. Use e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C and mₑ = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg.

items: Cathode rays are negatively charged and travel in straight lines.
Thermionic emission frees electrons from a hot metal.
An accelerating pd V gives each electron ½mv² = eV.

blocks.text: The specific charge of a particle is its charge divided by its mass. This section covers how Thomson found it for the electron.

items.meaning: Charge per unit mass of a particle, in C/kg. For the electron it is e ÷ mₑ, about 1.76 × 10¹¹ C/kg.

blocks.text: Any one method is enough. A common one uses a beam of electrons in a magnetic field.

items.text: Electrons are accelerated through a known pd V, so ½mv² = eV.
The beam enters a uniform magnetic field B at right angles. The magnetic force Bev is the centripetal force mv² ÷ r, so the path is a circle of radius r.
V and B are measured and r is read from the circular beam. Then e ÷ m is calculated.

items: The value of e ÷ mₑ was the same whatever the gas or the cathode metal. So the particles are the same in all matter.
The electron's specific charge is about **1800 times** bigger than that of the hydrogen ion.
If their charges are equal in size, the electron has about 1/1800 of the mass of a hydrogen atom.
So atoms are not the smallest particles: they contain much lighter particles.

sections.heading: Millikan and the charge on the electron

blocks.text: Millikan measured the charge on tiny oil droplets. This section covers the method and what it showed.

items.text: Charged oil droplets fall between two horizontal parallel plates a distance d apart.
A droplet falls at a terminal speed v, when its weight equals the viscous drag.
Stokes' law gives the drag, F = 6πηrv. At terminal speed the drag equals the weight, 6πηrv = mg, with m = 4⁄3πr³ρ for oil of density ρ. This gives the radius, and so the mass.
A pd V across the plates gives a field V ÷ d. The pd is adjusted until the droplet is held stationary.
At rest the electric force balances the weight: QV ÷ d = mg. So Q = mgd ÷ V.

blocks.label: Stokes' law
where: F = viscous force on the droplet (N)
η = viscosity of the air (N s m⁻²)

blocks.text: With the field on, a falling droplet can reach a terminal speed. For an upward electric force, QV ÷ d + 6πηrv = mg. The mass comes from the radius found without the field.

items: Every charge Millikan found was a whole-number multiple of 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
So electric charge is **quantised**: it comes in units of e and nothing smaller.
Knowing e and e ÷ mₑ, the mass of the electron can be worked out.
A stationary droplet has QV ÷ d = mg.
Stokes' law gives the radius from the terminal speed.
Charges are multiples of e, so charge is quantised.

checks.q: Explain how electrons are produced by thermionic emission.
checks.a: A current heats a metal filament or cathode. Free electrons gain enough energy to escape from its surface.

checks.q: An oil droplet of mass 2.7 × 10⁻¹⁵ kg is held stationary between plates 12 mm apart, with a pd of 2.0 kV across them. Calculate the charge on the droplet. (g = 9.81 N/kg)
State two conclusions from Thomson's and Millikan's experiments taken together.
checks.a: The electron is a very light particle, about 1/1800 of the mass of a hydrogen atom, so atoms contain smaller particles. Electric charge is quantised in units of e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.

blocks.text: Thermionic emission releases electrons from a heated metal. Fields then control them.

items: An **electric field** accelerates the electrons. A positive anode attracts them and each gains kinetic energy eV.
A **magnetic field** deflects them. The force is at right angles to their velocity, so the speed does not change and the path curves.
An electron gun uses both ideas: a heated cathode, an accelerating anode, then deflecting fields.
